utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before we resume with the testimony this morning, we have considered the motion on hearsay filed by the Defence and we heard arguments yesterday. We expect to render the decision sometime next week. In the meantime, we will continue to receive the testimony on the basis that we have been, that is, attempting to apply 89(C) which allows for the admission of all relevant evidence that has probative value. We will rule on any objections that the Defence may make and, consistent with the decision that we will issue next week, make any adjustments that are necessary depending upon what evidence is offered and the objection, if any, that is made. So, would you like to continue, please, Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If Mr. Mesic be recalled to the stand, please, and Mr. Kay is still cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am much obliged, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr. Kay, you are under cross-examination. Mr. Keegan does not need another opportunity at this point. MR. MESIC, recalled Cross-examined by MR. KAY, continued

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, you understand that you are still under the oath that you took yesterday? Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, I was asking you questions yesterday about the incident when the man called Kera was shot at Omarska camp. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want to go back to when the shot was fired. Did you go down to the ground at that stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you go down to the ground when you were told to or the crowd on the pista were told to by the guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did the guard tell you and the others to go down to the ground soon after the shot was fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, there was shooting and then we sat down, some walked and then we were told to sit down, and then when we sat down, when the gentleman came to us, he came to him, he greeted, they greeted each other, and then there was an order for us to lie down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where did the greeting between the two men take place? Where were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between the flower tubs and the lawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You did not know the man called Dusko Tadic yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never. I had never seen him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did others say the name "Tadic"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: They used that name itself, "Tadic"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Many other people were present and would also have seen what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you went to the ground, how were you positioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was next to the flower tubs. When everything was finished we were told to lie down and we laid down facing down and we could look -- we were able to look at the side a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were able to look aside a little bit your head was positioned looking down to the ground but, as you just indicated to the Court then, you were looking with a sideways glance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The man who gave the greeting, how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In uniform, camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Any other features of that uniform, the camouflage uniform, that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For instance, colour of the belt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was the appearance of the man? What did he look like? Can you remember his face? Can you describe that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a heavily built man and he had a big face.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Anything else about the face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have time to look.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So it seems then that this was not an opportunity for you to study carefully that other man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were worried about our lives, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, and you, no doubt, were worried and frightened at this time having seen a man shot in such a way so close to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Presumably, you were fearful of what else might happen in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only we were fearful, we expected it any minute, we expected someone to be called out and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Presumably, you felt that it was safer for you to follow the orders of those guards who were there on the pista?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So when you were told to look down to the ground, it was very important for you to follow that command and not be caught looking elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but one always looks what one wants to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, and you were-- I do not know if this translates -- stealing a glance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It did translate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you looked up again the man who gave the greeting was no longer there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later there was a command to stand up, we did so and I could not see him any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How much later was that when the command was given to stand up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You had not seen where the man had gone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You had not seen him leave the area where he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the period of time that you saw him was restricted to this greeting and then doing something with a notebook?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see him write anything, but he had it on his person. I do not know whether it was a book, a novel or a notebook, but I did not see him write anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you see if the book was opened or was it closed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was folded in his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You did not see him write anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next time you say you saw this man was the next day, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That was a day that you had to accompany a prisoner to the interrogation centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That was an occasion for some reason when you accompanied this person to the interrogation centre, perhaps you can tell us the reason why you had to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I was sitting next to him, and when someone was pointed at, he or she had to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But I do not quite understand why you had to go with this person to take them to the interrogation centre, what the purpose of that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was -- he had been beaten up. He was too weak to go on his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you were taking him, supporting him and delivering him where you were told?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You went into the interrogation centre and you went up the stairs, is that right, to the first floor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How did you know where to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guard was following us, sorry, in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At the top of the stairs did you go to an area where there was a corridor that ran along the building where there were rooms off the corridor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you remind me which room it was that you were taking the other prisoner to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the right-hand side, third door, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was the door to that room open or shut?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guard opened the door and took him in and left me behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Whereabouts were you left behind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Behind the other door, he came in and I was behind this other door in the corridor and raised three hands like this, and stood up facing the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long were you in that position for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up to about 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you remain like that whilst the other prisoner was being interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in that position but I also looked sideways. I stole glances and I saw the same person who had been there previously, the person who had greeted the guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you stole a glance and was the glance of this man on your left side or your right side when you saw him in another room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the right side, because I was turned, I just looked this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think you told us yesterday that he was sitting in another room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The man who had given the greeting the previous day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was a table in the corridor and chairs around it, and he lifted his feet on the table and was reclining in the chair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that place where he was positioned the same end of the corridor that you had entered from the stairs up to the first floor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is an area on the first floor where the table and chairs are positioned on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you had not walked past that table and those chairs on your way up into the corridor when you first arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we had, and the second or third room, we left it. They then pulled me back and placed me against the wall and asked me to raise three fingers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you had not seen the man sitting at that table when you had first come into the corridor, you had not walk past him before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had. Yes, I took a glance and then I was frightened myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I thought you told us that you saw him when you were standing against the wall with your three fingers up against the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I looked, I stole a glance at him too at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No doubt during your period in Omarska you saw many guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You saw many people at that camp who were not prisoners ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- but were people who were connected with the business of the camp either as guards or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were interrogators. We saw them in the offices where they interrogated us in the rooms and there were also the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell me how long it was that you were a prisoner in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember exactly. I was there close to two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Then after those two months did you go to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long were you at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know when the camp was disbanded, when the Omarska camp was disbanded. Then they put us on buses and we were taken to Manjaca. From Manjaca, I was released due to my sickness, to an illness, on the 25th. I have a card, a piece of paper, when I was released from Trnopolje, and that is how I remember that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So would it be right to say that you were in Manjaca for about 20 days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, but it is written when I left Omarska and when I went to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you say the 25th, do you mean 25th August was the day that you were released from Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You left Omarska at about the time that the camp was closing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: After Manjaca you spent a few days in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two days in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Then after Trnopolje did you return to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where you stayed for nearly a year, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From August until June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: About nine months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You told the Court yesterday that you had not seen any news coverage from newspapers or television concerning the case of Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I had not, or am I able to watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The first photographs shown to you were last month in June of 1996, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: About four years after the incidents that you describe taking place in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Since your leaving Bosnia-Herzegovina, you have been living in a country which has television and newspapers, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You first made a statement concerning these events that you describe in Omarska in January of this year, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have you made any other statements to anyone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: After you had left Bosnia-Herzegovina did you not take an interest in allegations being made against the Serbian people in the news of the country where you live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I was ill, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But, presumably, you still had your ability to watch television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but I did not speak the language of the country I was staying in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, but you are able to watch pictures on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not, I was ill, as I said, and even to this day I have been keeping away from all things political.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Even when this case started in May of this year, did you not watch television to see what was happening in the case where you were going to be involved and a witness against ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you have been walking around the streets in the country where you have been living, you have been able to see newspaper stalls or shops that sell magazines and newspapers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not speak the language and I am not interested in reading newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is not a question of not speaking the language, it is being able to see the pictures of someone who has been on the cover of magazines and on the front page of newspapers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you telling us that you have not seen any pictures of Dusko Tadic in the country where you have been living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And when you come to look at an album of photographs four years after those events in Omarska that you had not seen a picture of that man before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because what I suggest to you is this, that when you were shown that photograph album in June of this year you had seen other photographs of the man charged before this court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was given those photographs to see how many there were, how many criminals there were. I recognised the person on the fourth picture because I had seen that person twice before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you had seen many other people in Omarska for longer periods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What I suggest to you is that you are not telling us the truth about having avoided all photographs and information in the newspapers and on television about this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, there have been many of my family have been killed, and I was not able to look at anything related to that war. How would you behave if you had three of your brother's sons killed or and one nephew? How would you respond to that situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is why I am questioning your answers on this matter and understanding the harm that you have suffered, but the point is because of those things that have been so painful to you, are you, in fact, determined to not tell the truth about what you have seen because of the anger you feel about what has wrongly happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not looking at anything and I refuse to look at anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yet, despite that cutting off, as you say, from information or looking at things, you were still prepared to offer yourself as a witness in the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wanted to and I still want only to say the truth about what people did, and the kind of terror against the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, and because of that motivation, has that caused you to be determined to do your bit, as you see it, to say something about a Serb charged in this court even though you did not see him as you claim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, is it difficult for you to think about the events which occurred in Bosnia to you and to your family and to others in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Is it difficult for you to talk about those events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Since you left Bosnia have you tried to avoid thinking about and having to talk about those events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I went to see the doctor and I still go to see a psychiatrist, and I have been told whenever I walk to walk by the water and always have somebody accompany me, to steady my nerves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Has it also been difficult on your wife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Has she, in fact, recently had a heart attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A stroke.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you were approached by members of the Tribunal, did you feel it was your duty to come and give testimony as requested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my duty and my conscience told me that I had to come, that I had to come and to tell the truth, what is true and not what is a lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: It is not the case that you hold what happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina to you and your family against all Serbs; in fact you already in this court stated that you wanted to protect the identity of a Serb who helped you during that time, is that not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I shall protect him always and I will send him money.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you remember the faces of some of the other guards in that camp and some of the other prisoners in that camp after all this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I did remember many of them and I know their faces, but I do not know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you recalling Kera Crnalic shot on the pista, that was a very significant event to you, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a heavy blow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In fact, I believe your testimony yesterday was that you had never seen anyone killed that way before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You still carry that memory with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My Lords, if and when I talk about this I feel bad. I do not feel like talking about it because all those images come back to me from Omarska, from Manjaca. They are all before my eyes -- even now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The image of that shooting that you have includes the face of the guard who killed Kera as well as the man who was identified to you as Tadic, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Always.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You got a clear look at that man's face, the man identified to you as Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: With respect to my learned friend, I think that these series of questions ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- have been of an extent of leading a witness that is unacceptable and that the conclusion should come from the witness, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I will sustain the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you were in the hallway in the administration building the next day after the shooting ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: -- were you able to get a clear look at the face of the man sitting at the table in the corridor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Are you sure that was the same man you had seen the day before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sure -- yes, it is gospel truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Nothing further, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, recross?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Witness, I have one question to ask you, I do not think it has emerged as yet: you said yesterday that they took your brother away and three of his sons, and it says in the transcript a brother of a son. That seems to be an error, perhaps, but have you seen any of those family members since then again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have just one question, Mr. Mesic, do you recall the approximate date that you were taken to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us the month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Additional questions, Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: To clarify that, your Honour, I think we can clarify it in relation to events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, are you able to tell the Court approximately how many days after the attack on Hambarine you were taken to Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four or five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: To follow up one additional question, you indicated that yesterday approximately how many days were you in the small garage before you went to interrogation and were placed on the pista?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 25 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, has the date of the attack on Hambarine been identified through this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Certainly other witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I was really trying to place this in context. I think I can do it by looking at other witnesses. Fine. Thank you very much. Mr. Kay, do you have additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to Mr. Mesic being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, you are permanently excused. That means you may leave and thank you very much for coming today and yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: While the next witness is coming, could you just remind me of the date of the attack on Hambarine, if you have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 23rd May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is a witness who is under conditions of protection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, I forgot. Thank you for reminding me. Excuse me one minute. The next witness has been granted protective measures that will, inter alia, allow the image distortion of his face, but he will testify in the Court room. In order to give this witness the full protection that has been ordered, we will need to stand in recess for five or 10 minutes for the blinds to be lowered. The witness will then be brought in and the necessary adjustments will be made. So we will stand in recess for 10 minutes

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Witness R was called

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, you may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. R, could you take a look at the name on this piece of paper and indicate if that is your correct name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Bos, if you could please show that to Mr. Wladimiroff? Sir, in what year were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on 7th June 1964.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You were raised in Prijedor in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you attend primary and secondary school there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you serve your compulsory military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In what year was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What were you trained as during your military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a military policeman, trained as a military policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After your compulsory military service, did you do any reserve military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the reserve force of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How many times did you do reserve service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it happened -- once I did a longer drill of a month, a month and something, and there were also cases when we would be called up for a day only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: For how many years did you do this reserve service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, until 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After that were you excused from military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for reasons of health.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During the time that you lived in Prijedor after your military service, what was your profession or occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Commerce. I was a trader, a merchant, a salesman in stores of a supermarket kind, self-service stores, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you also have training as a butcher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, more or less you might say that I could work as a butcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When did you stop working in the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stopped working in Prijedor on 25th May '92. That is when my work record was closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Why was your work record closed? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one day I was told off, the work, and on that day I no longer performed my professional duties, and the explanation that is in my work record, job record, which I collected from my company, there was this explanation, one of the explanations, was because of the rebellion against the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What part of the town of Prijedor did you live in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The part of the town, the so-called Stari Grad, old town, well-known.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you arrested at your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What date was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May 30th all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Sir, can you describe how that arrest took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on 30th May early in the morning, and it was early, very early, we could hear gunfire and bursts and detonations over a broader area around Stari Grad, and this gunfire was coming ever closer. We did not go out. We simply switched on the radio and we heard Radio Prijedor, its programme, and it was informing us that all citizens should hoist up white flags in order to mark their house and that citizens should not be concerned about their security, that allegedly a group of Muslim extremists had attacked the town of Prijedor and that shortly, if at all, it would all come under the reliable control of the army of Republika Srpska, and that is how it was. We spent the whole day in the house and the different detonations were coming ever closer and ever stronger. It was the fire from tanks which were laying waste to the town, and so we stayed in the house until half past 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you put out some sort of a white flag in front of your house, as the radio indicated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my brother put up a white flag on the hedge, on the boundary, on the hedge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What later happened at your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A very short while later, it was in the afternoon around half past 4, we had a very wide door on the house which was not locked because we were expecting somebody to appear there any moment, and that is how it was two soldiers turned up. They kicked the door open, and they entered and in a very aggressive language, "Your balija mother, fuck you, Alija", and so on, "Get out" and we all went out in a very disciplined way. Nobody even thought, dared to think, let alone try to do something, and when we came out in the street there were already our neighbours, well-known people also and several soldiers in uniforms, uniforms of the Yugoslav People's Army who had arm bands, white, and had still the old JNA caps on their heads. Some had the five pointed stars and some had fur hats, very tall with Chetnik markings, with kokardas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What type of uniforms were those people wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some had SMB uniforms and some even the camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You said your neighbours were also being rounded up. What type of people were they rounding up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In that part there were only two Serb households, all the others were Muslims. There was the house of Zeljko married to a Muslim woman, and a lad whom we called Mandala who still lives in the old town and he now lives in Dzemal's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In the street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the street they were all Muslims, old children, we, the adults of various ages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: On the translation it says "Muslim old children", did you intend to say "Muslim old and children"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Old people and children, they were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: From your street where were the people taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We started from that street to Cerica Sokak. We passed by Djogo Dzemal's house and went down by lime trees to the River Sana. In front of us were the Prijedor bridge and the Prijedor Hotel, so we went down below the lime trees and reached the concrete bridge in front of the garden restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: From the bridge where was everyone taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the bridge, we were standing there as tanks were parked there and trucks with canisters on them with new Bosnian plates; and from thence we went across the bridge on the Berek. We went to a place called Ciganuluk where there were blacksmiths and we passed by the house of Suljo Garnic and reached the park in front of the town hall of Prijedor where there was a monument to Mladen Stojanovic and we spent in that park sometime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What happened in the park?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the park which was planted with birches, with birch trees, there were more armed uniformed soldiers whom we found there, and there after a very short while they separated us, the men over the age of 15 from their wives and mothers and children, and we headed for SUP; and they were sent to the sports hall, "Mladost", which was in the immediate vicinity of the police building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. R, you said "they were sent to the sports hall", who was "they"? Who were sent to the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were, displaced children below the age of 15 and old people and women, just even as my wife and my two-year and two years and 27 days old child was also sent there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where were the men taken in the SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We, who were separated there, were sent in the direction of SUP, the so-called police. As we were entering the SUP, there were quite a number of soldiers and policemen, different, who served there, who worked there. As we were passing through the lobby or the corridor of the police station, we had to pass through a cordon of officers -- of soldiers and policemen who beat us ruthlessly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You said that they were a cordon of soldiers and policemen, how could you tell the difference between who was a soldier and who was a policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I could; soldiers were in SMB uniforms and camouflage clothes and the policemen wore blue uniforms and looked much tidier, much neater, than the soldiers. I knew quite a lot of those policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You recognised some of those policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of the Reserve Police strength there was Radic from Urije called "Grga" who work for Drustrena Ishrana in Ljubija. Drustrena Ishrana of the Ljubija mine which was in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The people that you recognised there, what ethnic group were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbs, of Serb descent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After you passed through that cordon of police and soldiers, where were you taken in the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When in the station we were taken into the -- on the grounds of the military police where they kept their cars and vehicles and trucks, and there was a building something like a warehouse for armaments and storage, and it was as one went out from the lobby one faced directly that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That area described by some as a "courtyard"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a courtyard closed from one side. On one side there was a high concrete wall with barbed wired, and the entrance had sliding doors with one ball, with one ball bearing so that they could move.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Once you were in that courtyard area, what were you told to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The orders were to stand with our arms spread and lean with three fingers against a wall which was very rough against this wall, and that is what we had to do. Then we had to take off our shoes, everything, we had to be bare foot, and that is how we stood there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What occurred then, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What occurred then, very horrible things occurred then. Whoever passed by beat us. They paid no attention if he was a young man or an old man. They did that and throw invectives at us -- horrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What were you beaten with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the police baton to boards to planks, all sorts of objects, boots, batons across the kidneys, the spine, the neck, genitals. They trod on our feet -- everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you told to sing while you were in the courtyard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were ordered to sing. We all kept silent and then one of those military there yelled at us and said, "Now you are going to sing? You have had enough of your Muslim songs".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did you sing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we simply of all the Serb propaganda that we heard day in and day out, it occurred to us to sing the Serb song "Who says who lies that Serbia is small", and we sang it and a whole choir sang it. I mean, each one sang it for himself but they were quite happy with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: While you were in that courtyard at one point did you take the opportunity to look up at the windows above in the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the window of the police building there was Simo Miskovic -- a tall man, very smart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you know what his position was in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was a member of the SDS and he also had his coffee bar in the Mrakovica cinema, in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How long approximately do you believe you were in that courtyard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were there until about 8.00, half past 8, for some two or three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: From that courtyard where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken to buses which were already waiting ready for things like that, just as all my neighbours were taken away by those buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How were you told to sit in those buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a man would board that bus and there were up to four persons in seats meant for two, and we also had to bend our heads very low, almost below the seats so that the buses from the outside looked as empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where did you end up after that bus trip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We ended up next to the Balkan Hotel where there were other citizens of Muslim descent who were also boarded on to those buses. Then we went on also in front of the police, and we followed the so-called Celuloska Street by the pulp and paper factory. That is what we named it after. We passed the factory and came out to the bank of the Sana River, and then we turned left and then we crossed the bridge on the Gomjenica River and went through the so-called Serb Gomjenica and then we went through Cela, Sanicani and followed the high street. Then we turned left off the main road towards a place called Maricka, and then we headed for Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you arrived at Omarska and were taken off the buses what occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we were getting off the buses, and it was a very slow business because we all had to be searched. So when the first bus was unboarded, all men had to stand against the wall also with their arms and legs spread as they were searched one by one. Then out of the blue two soldiers turned up and they fired a burst of -- they fired a burst of fire and two men fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Two men, what two men? Were they detainees or were they policemen or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those were prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you were taken off the bus where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were also taken towards that wall, and then two guards came with two buckets of water and washed away the blood as if nothing had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you also searched while you were against the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were searched and directed towards the building against which we had been leaning. In the corridor we were met by a clerk, a fair boy, shortish, and a young man whom I knew very well because of all the sports and games. His nickname was Djaja and I think he had his video store I believe it was in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: This Djaja, what did he do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He took our particulars, noted them down, the name, the date of birth and where we came from -- everything that is normally on an ID card.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After you gave your particulars to him, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the extension as one passes by that table, there was a large room. It looked very cold. It was desolate and that is where I found my neighbours and my acquaintances from the first bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What building what was that room in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in the administrative building against which we had to lean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How many days did you end up spending in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, about 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did that room have a name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was that room called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was called "Mujo's room". It was named after another prisoner, inmate, Mujo Crnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Why was it named after that prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why it was named after him because the guards, some of the superiors, some of those supposed to maintain order amongst us, he was responsible for us, he took us to lunch every day in columns of 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that would be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We understood that you would need about 45 minutes for direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That is an estimate, your Honour. Since we are not getting to the critical part, I am more than happy to carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is fine. I do not know about cross-examination. We can stand in recess for 20 minutes then.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): Mr. R, when we broke for the recess you indicated you had been in Mujo's room, I believe, for about 20 days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: From Mujo's room where did you go in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that everybody from that room was sent to the place called "pista", which is outside the administration building where we had been staying on the ground floor, and there was some sorting out at that point. The minors and the old people and the sickly people who had problems with health, they had priority to enter that room and that is how it happened. The others remained on the pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: By that room do you mean Mujo's room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I mean Mujo's room.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: While you were on the pista were you taken for an interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How did that come about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On some days there had been very rapid interrogations and some strange and hard things happened. We were all frightened because we had seen all these people coming back from interrogation in a very, very bad condition, covered with blood. Some of them were brought in blankets, carried in blankets, and they all said that in such cases, "We want two strong men to carry this person" and we knew from that that someone had been beaten up very, very badly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did you do as a result of seeing all of these things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was looking at that, watching that with my own eyes, I just, I simply wanted either to survive or to have the same fate of the previous ones and that is what I did. I had seen a guard with a police uniform, a blue uniform. He seemed very different from the others. He did not have any weapons on his person and he was unarmed. One day I made a decision. I walked up to him. He had a nickname, that is what we called him by, Kole. I walked up to him and asked him, "Is there any possibility for me to be called out so that I can have that worry, get over that worry?" He said he will look into that and I wrote my name and gave it to him on a piece of paper, and after a certain time he came out and called me out and then I followed him to the office, to the interrogation office, which was on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: So the interrogation office you were taken to was on the ground floor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was an office on the ground floor. The others were around the circular staircase leading up to the upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the person who interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the person who interrogated me when I entered the office, I simply entered the office and sat down in a chair, he addressed me and said, "You have already sat down". Then I jumped up again. I said, "I can stand up if I sat down". He said, "No problem, just keep sitting". There was another person with him. Then he introduced himself to me. He said, "My name is Balaban, I am from Banja Luka" -- a young man about 36 or 38 years old, tall, blond, handsome you might say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What type of questions did he ask you during this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During this interrogation he asked me questions about where I was from, what I did for a living, what I had been working as a civilian, doing as a civilian, mostly easy questions. He asked me also if I went fishing, if I went fishing, I said, yes; if I had a hobby -- they were mostly easy questions -- if I was a member of a political party; I said I had never been interested in politics, and I had never been a member of the presidency of the youth organisation. The only political thing I did was my pledge as a pioneer. I had never been a member of the Communist Party of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did he ask you about any particular people from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he mentioned Dedo Crnalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did he ask you about Dedo Crnalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He asked me if I knew him, if I had gone to his cafe, "yes", I said, "I had been there", we used to gather together there, although there were one or two other cafes near Dedo's cafe. He asked me what sort of people met there and what they had talked about. I said I had not been interested in that; on one occasion he asked me to work for him in the cafe and I refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you beaten during this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was only one person, a tall man. He walked behind my back and every moment I expected him to hit me. I was very tense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After the interrogation what did this Balaban tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Balaban told me that I should not worry at all, that I would spend the rest of my time there peacefully, that I was not one of those people who belonged to the groups, as they called them, first, second and third group, and he said, "You are in the third group". I did not understand anything about these numbers, first, second or third group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: From the interrogation where did you return to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I returned to the pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How long did you spend on the pista then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent a certain period of time, so I was returned to Mujo's room again and after a large number of names were called I was transferred to the hangar, to the room where the heavy coal mining machinery was located, dump trucks, etc.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you were returned to Mujo's room did you find a place in that room where you could lay down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did find myself a place. It was a very, very small space. There was very hardly any space at all, but I had to simply make do with what I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was that space that you found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the place in the toilet itself. On the grill where boots were washed and there were three taps there, one of which was working. During the entire day we stood there because water was very important, very much in need, and during the night one individual who was nicknamed "Doc" or "Doctor", he worked in the work brigade, he had a pair of pliers, and every night he closed the tap so that I could sleep there and there were three of us sleeping at that grill, three of us like sardines, lined up like sardines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. R. If I could have this photo marked as the next exhibit in order -- that will be 244 -- and handed to the witness, please? (To the witness): Mr. R, do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is the photograph showing the area right next to the entrance to the toilet, the only door to the toilet, and behind there were three toilets which were always blocked. There was excrement all over the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Is that the grate where you spent your nights?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, nights, many nights.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does the Defence have a copy of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I do not believe they have an actual copy of the photograph. They were shown the photograph, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. MR. KEEGAN (To the witness): Mr. R, please, if you would stand in your spot, I would remind you, please, to move slowly when you stand, and if you could use that pointer in front of you and point on the model the area known as Mujo's room -- using the model, please? Stand and point on the model where Mujo's room was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the entrance to Mujo's room, as in front outside there were two big tubs with taps on top and in the middle there was a metal grill, so that the workers were able to wash their boots and all the mud went through because there was a pipe taking this dirty water down. This was the entrance to Mujo's room, A5, and right next to it there was a door, there was the WC, the toilet. The room here is marked as A4, as far as I can see. This area was Mujo's room. There was a small room here. We called it the "gentlemen's room" because that is where Dedo Crnalic was, Asif Kapetanovic, Mursel and Esad Sadikovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Sir, while you are still standing with the pointer, could you also point to the area in the hangar building where you said you were taken after you were moved out of Mujo's room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I was taken out of Mujo's room -----

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Move back a little bit. I realise it is difficult. You cannot lean over too far, that is all:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a third door here. This is where the dumpers were parked and in this area there was barbed wired, about three strands of barbed wired, and on the left-hand side there was an old demper with a machine gun on top of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During the time that you were on the pista, did you ever see a man who was identified to you as Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you describe those circumstances to the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, while on one occasion we were sitting on the pista, there was a large number there, one individual from the area of Kozarac was sitting in my immediate vicinity and so we were talking, chatting. The only topic was, are we going back home today, tomorrow? That individual sitting next to me pointed out to me, said, "That is Dusko". I did not pay any attention. He bent down and I turned my head towards the white house. At that moment Dusko was coming out of the white house. The person, the individual, passed. He went left behind the house to a lawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: First off, this area behind the white house, what was kept there or put there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were mostly bodies there. Sometimes those bodies would remain there for the whole day and the following morning a small lorry would transport them out of the area. It was sort of orange yellow colour -- more orange than yellow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Before the war did you personally know a man named Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only from the media, from the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: This man who was sitting next to you who you say was from Kozarac, do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember his surname, but I cannot remember his name. Hrnic was his surname, as far as I remember. Yes, I remember this quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you saw this man come out of the white house and he was identified to you as Dusko, did you have any recognition when you saw the man, saw his face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a few moments I created the impression from the newspapers, the image came to my mind, a picture, mostly on the sports page of the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What do you mean a picture came to your mind from the sports page of the paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the sports column which was published weekly in the newspaper Kozarski Vjesnik, which was a weekly, and there was a lot of sports news, handball, basketball, judo, karate. There were individual sports treated in that on that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What picture did you have in your mind that you had seen before, what did it relate to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had remembered because at that time young people having seen many karate films had decided to become karate people, karate sportsmen, and that was the section on karate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you saw the man identified to you as Dusko come out of the white house, did you get a clear look at his face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my view was not obstructed at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you recall what that man was wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was wearing a multi-coloured jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did the pattern of that jacket remind you of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The multi-coloured jacket reminded me of the colour of the skin of a giraffe, the colour of a giraffe hide, skin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After you saw the man identified to you as Dusko on that day, did you ever see him again in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During the time you were in the camp did you ever spend any time in the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on a July day, on a day in July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Why were you in the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That day after lunch we were sitting on the pista, it was very, very hot and humid and suddenly there was a summer shower, so we were separated into two groups. One group went to room 15 in the hangar and some of us went to the white house, in the direction of the white house, to the two rooms in the back and a toilet which had not been finished yet in the white house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: While you were in the white house, did you witness any beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you describe the beating that you witnessed on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That day we were in the white house, in those two rooms and one toilet which had not been completed yet. We had a very painful time, because we passed the prisoners, the inmates, who had been placed in the left room as you go into the white house, both the room to the left and to the right. After a short time three individuals appeared at the door, Duca Knezevic, Zeljko Timarac and followed by, following them was Emir Ramic nicknamed "Hankin". The order was, "I want half of the space emptied". That is what we did. We all crammed into one corner, so there was a large area that was empty. Then Duca was holding a baton in his hand and Emir was standing in front of him. He had a list in his hand and was looking for one individual. Then he went from one person to another hitting them on the head, "What is your name? Where are you from?" We all said normally, "I am from such and such a place" until he came to a person about 42 or 45 years old, a shorter person, who was wearing a leather jacket. He was with us, and Duca asked him, "What is your name?" He said, "Dalija Hrnic". "How come you are here? Fuck your mother. Go to this other room and wait for me". Dalija said, "You must have confused me with somebody else". "I do not want to know anything. Just go over to this other room", and he did. He asked us all these questions. Nothing happened to us after that. Then he asked Emir Ramic, "Do you know these people here?" He said, "No, I do not. They are people from the country". That is what Emir answered. Then there was a very, very strong blow with a baton across the entire head. There was blood all over him. He was very smartly dressed. He was wearing a white shirt, a summer shirt. He looked awful. He fell down immediately. Then Zeljko threw him out and told him to wait outside the white house on the left-hand side. Emir was standing there. Then they went into the small room of the white house where there were some other prisoners who looked awful, horrible. There was blood on the walls, on the tiles, all over the place. Then Duca and Zeljko went into the small room and started beating people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Which room of the white house was that, sir, that small room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first on the left as you enter the white house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did that room have a name, did the prisoners have a name for that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, everybody called it shock room, like intensive care room, because the people looked awful who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You said that Duca and Zeljko were in that room and started beating people. What could you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was standing outside the door to the small room. Then Zeljko and Duca came in and started beating Dalija Hrnic. There was Becir Medunjanin there whom they kicked like an old ball. They kicked him out into the corridor. The man was lying down on his back. Then Zeljko Timarac started beating him up really badly, really cruelly. He was jumping on his chest. My impression was that his boot came all the way down to the floor when he jumped on his chest. He did not say anything to Becir. He was almost, he was almost out of his consciousness and he had blood and foam coming out of his mouth, trickling down. It was horrible. Then Timarac picked him up by his feet and drew him, dragged him back into the small room. Then we were thrown out and Emir was returned to the small room. We were returned to the pista because the rain had stopped. Then there were two shots, two handgun shots. After that I never saw Emir Ramic again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. R, do you know the full name of that man you have referred to as "Duca"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that person is called Dusko or Duca Knezevic from Orlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you know that man before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had heard from my coworkers about him, since he is older than I am, in my profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Had you actually met him before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had seen him in passing, but I never spent any time with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was there any similarity physically between he and the man who was identified to you as "Tadic"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just one matter, the witness did not, as I understood it and as I recollect -- I may be wrong about this -- have identified as "Tadic".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He said "Dusko".

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am grateful to your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, you understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I understand it was Dusko, which he then said, "and then I had the picture in my mind that it was Dusko Tadic whom I had seen in the paper". Yes, your Honour, you are correct that he was identified as "Dusko". (To the witness): What was the physical build of this man, Duca Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Duca?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he had a pot belly. He was heavily built. He was short -- I could not tell you how tall he was -- and rather broad shoulders. He had a big stomach.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In your opinion, was there any similarity between the face of the man Duca Knezevic and the man identified to you as Dusko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How long did you spend in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent the time from 30th May until 6th August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Just prior to your leaving the camp, did visitors come to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who were those visitors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Newspaper people and cameramen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where were you taken from Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Omarska I was about 700, 720 or 730 of us were transferred to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How much time did you spend in the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: While you were in the Trnopolje camp were you given any jobs to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No jobs, but we had to make ourselves a tent so we could sleep, we would have a shelter so we would not be out in the open.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where did you get the materials to make the shelter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The material was given to us from the wire, the fence that had been used to fence in the entire camp of Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That fencing was taken down and then used by the people to build shelters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were mostly reinforcement steel for use in construction, square grills, and we used them to make a mini igloo which could have been bent into an arch, and then we had to press it down with stones so that it would not bend back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After you left the Trnopolje camp where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I returned to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: While you were in Prijedor did you have a chance to see the area or town known as Stari Grad again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you describe what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came to Prijedor, we had already heard in Omarska it had been raised to the ground, and one day I went to Sanski Most and the bridge which linked Tukovi and the town, and one could see everything from that bridge. It was autumn. There were no leaves or anything. All one could see were three residential buildings, houses, there. Only Dzemal Djogo's house, a man who worked for the biscuit factory, was still surviving. His wife used to work at the medical centre. Then another house was the old building which we used to call "Lovac", "Hunter", because it housed the hunters' club on the upper floor and on the ground floor there was a coffee bar. Next to the bridge at the entrance into Stari Grad there was a summer garden. Once upon a time there was a summer, an open air cinema and discotheque. Those were the only three buildings and to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could Exhibit 79, the map of Prijedor, be given to the witness, please, and placed on the elmo? Could you zoom in closer, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. R, using the pointer, could you point out on the map next to you, not on the screen, where Stari Grad is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the ethnic group of the population who lived in that area before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that part the ethnic group was Muslim, most 100 per cent, except that I said that Zeljko lived there in a mixed marriage, and the person that I mentioned, Mandala, his name is Milan. There was nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In June of this year were you shown a book of photographs by an investigator from the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did that book have a number on its cover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you remember what that number was?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If I could have this marked as the next Exhibit in order which, I believe, would be 245 and handed to the witness? While that is being done, your Honour, I would tender Exhibit 244 which was the photograph which I neglected to do earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to 244?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The same as the previous objection, your Honour; it is an ongoing objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: 244 was just the photograph of the grate.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is the photograph of the grate, the grate in the -- 244 was the grate where the witness testified that he slept with some other prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: There is no objection to that one, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is OK. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I apologise, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No problem. MR. KEEGAN (To the witness): Mr. R, if you could look at that book, please, which has been given to you and tell me if you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Is that the book shown to you by the investigator from the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When the investigator handed you that book what did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All he said was to look at this album. He said nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you look at each picture in the book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the whole sequence very carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you recognise any photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Whose photograph did you recognise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the photograph which is the 11th here and that is the photograph of Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The photograph, is that the man who was identified to you as "Dusko" in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After you identified that photograph for the investigator, did you do anything else with the book, with the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I signed on the back of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I would offer Exhibit 245, your Honour. A copy has already been provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, the objection, the standing objection, that you have to the use of the photospread, that will be overruled. Exhibit 245 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. R, is there any doubt in your mind that the photograph of the man you identified in the book is the same man whom you saw in Omarska camp that was identified to you as "Dusko"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no doubts at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Cross-examination, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. R, when were you first asked to be a witness in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell me the date that you were first asked to become a witness in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it this year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had you ever made a statement to anyone else about matters with which you were concerned in Omarska before you gave any statement to the Prosecution in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No one else, except on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
